evidence: Fresh independent exact enumeration of one-, two-, and three-edge subsets on primes through 29.
correctness.rationale: Encoding semiprime denominators as edges of a simple prime-support graph is exact. The target prime p must occur. Multiplication by the product of support primes and reduction modulo any other support prime excludes every non-p leaf. Hence one and two edges are impossible, while a three-edge graph containing p must be the triangle on p,q,r. Its unit-fraction identity reduces exactly to qr=q+r+p, or (q-1)(r-1)=p+1. For p=1 mod 4, the product is 2 mod 4, forcing one factor to be 1 and thus one auxiliary prime to be 2. A fresh finite exact-arithmetic replay on the first ten primes found nine three-edge hits, all and only triangle-factor cases, and no one- or two-edge hits.
risks: When the factorization fails, the theorem gives only lambda(p)>=4; it does not determine the next possible length.

evidence: Complete length-three classification for every prime target.
Exact connection to twin primes in one residue class.
value.rationale: This is the first nontrivial shortest-length question for the simplest squarefree targets not themselves allowable denominators. The exact triangle criterion and the twin-prime collapse on p=1 mod 4 give a clean arithmetic classification tied directly to the newly solved semiprime Egyptian-fraction problem.
risks: No density theorem for qualifying primes and no exact lambda(p) beyond length three.

final_claim: For a prime p, a distinct-squarefree-semiprime Egyptian representation of 1/p has minimum length three exactly when p+1=(q-1)(r-1) for distinct primes q,r different from p; every three-term representation is the triangle {pq,pr,qr}, and for p congruent to 1 modulo 4 this is equivalent to p+2 being prime.
limitations: No exact larger minimum when the factorization fails.
